title: AP Music Theory
summary: Read pitch and rhythm, analyse tonal harmony and explain musical structure.
frameworkNote: Checked against the official eight-unit sequence on 15 October 2026 for 2026-27. These original text exercises support notation and analysis. They do not replace audio dictation, sight-singing, score study or teacher feedback. Pitch names use scientific octave labels where needed.

modules.title: Count beats and spell a major scale
modules.focus: Connect pitch order to meter and beat division.
explanation: A major scale follows whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half steps. Use each letter name once before repeating the tonic. A key signature supplies consistent alterations; an accidental changes a note according to notation conventions within its measure.

Meter groups beats, while rhythm describes durations within that grouping. In simple meter a beat divides into two; in compound meter it divides into three. Six-eight commonly groups six eighth notes into two dotted-quarter beats, so counting six equal pulses alone misses the usual larger organisation.

workedExample.prompt: Spell D major and identify the usual beats in 6/8.
steps: Apply the step pattern: D E F-sharp G A B C-sharp D.
Group the six eighth notes as 3 + 3, giving two dotted-quarter beats.

misconception.claim: The top meter number always equals the number of felt beats.
misconception.correction: Compound meter commonly groups three subdivisions into each beat.

questions.prompt: Spell F major.
questions.hint: The fourth scale degree requires an accidental.
questions.answer: F G A B-flat C D E F.

questions.prompt: How many eighth notes fit one dotted quarter?
questions.hint: A dot adds half the original value.
questions.answer: Three eighth notes: two for the quarter plus one for its dot.

questions.prompt: Spell B-flat major.
hints: Place semitones between degrees three-four and seven-eight.
questions.answer: B-flat C D E-flat F G A B-flat. E-flat preserves the fourth-degree letter. The pattern has semitones D–E-flat and A–B-flat.
checkpoints: B-flat C D E-flat F G A B-flat.
The pattern has semitones D–E-flat and A–B-flat.

questions.prompt: Explain why six quarter notes do not by themselves identify a metre.
questions.answer: The total duration is six quarter notes. It could be grouped in different metres or across bars. Accent, notation and context are needed to establish metre.
checkpoints: The total duration is six quarter notes.
It could be grouped in different metres or across bars.
Accent, notation and context are needed to establish metre.

notes.title: Count beats and spell a major scale in depth
paragraphs: Scale spelling combines letter sequence with interval size. Starting on A-flat, the major pattern requires A-flat, B-flat, C, D-flat, E-flat, F, G and A-flat; replacing D-flat with C-sharp would preserve a piano key but obscure the required fourth scale degree. Meter then organises duration at a different level. In 9/8, the usual compound grouping is three dotted-quarter beats, each divided into three eighth notes. Beaming and accents can confirm or challenge an assumed grouping. A correct total duration alone does not explain how a listener perceives the beat.

workedExamples.prompt: Spell E-flat major and group one ordinary 9/8 bar of nine eighth notes.
steps: Use consecutive letters E F G A B C D E, then apply the major pattern: E-flat F G A-flat B-flat C D E-flat.
Group the eighths 3+3+3, giving three dotted-quarter beats.
workedExamples.conclusion: Pitch spelling and metrical grouping solve separate parts of the task.

flashcards.front: What is the fourth degree of E-flat major?
What is the major step pattern?
How many usual beats are in 9/8?
Why avoid repeated letter names in a scale?
flashcards.back: Each scale degree needs its own letter.

diagrams.title: Compound triple grouping
diagrams.description: Nine subdivisions form three larger beats.

nodes.label: Groups of three
nodes.detail: Each group forms a dotted quarter.

modules.title: Distinguish minor forms and textures
modules.focus: Track altered scale degrees and independent lines.
explanation: Natural minor has lowered third, sixth and seventh degrees relative to parallel major. Harmonic minor raises the seventh to create a leading tone. The conventional ascending melodic minor also raises the sixth; its conventional descending form returns to natural minor.

Texture concerns how musical layers relate. Monophony has one melodic line, even if doubled at the octave. Homophony often combines a principal melody with accompaniment. Polyphony involves multiple independent melodic lines. Instrument count alone cannot determine texture, and a written label still needs confirmation through score or listening evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Compare A natural minor and A harmonic minor.
steps: Write A B C D E F G A for natural minor.
Raise G to G-sharp in harmonic minor, creating a semitone approach to A.

misconception.claim: Minor always means slower or sadder music.
misconception.correction: Mode describes pitch relationships; tempo and expressive effect depend on additional choices.

questions.prompt: Spell ascending A melodic minor.
questions.answer: A B C D E F-sharp G-sharp A.

questions.prompt: Ten singers perform the same melody in octaves. What texture is this?
questions.answer: Monophonic, because there is one melodic line doubled at the octave.
checkpoints: Does not infer polyphony from numbers

questions.prompt: Spell D harmonic minor.
questions.answer: D E F G A B-flat C-sharp D. C-sharp is the leading tone. B-flat remains the sixth degree.
checkpoints: D E F G A B-flat C-sharp D.

questions.prompt: A violin and flute play the same melody an octave apart. Explain the texture.
questions.answer: The two instruments double one melodic line. That can be monophonic texture. Two instruments alone do not establish polyphony.
checkpoints: The two instruments double one melodic line.
Two instruments alone do not establish polyphony.

notes.title: Distinguish minor forms and textures in depth
paragraphs: Minor forms alter specific scale degrees rather than changing every pitch. In E natural minor the notes are E F-sharp G A B C D E. Harmonic minor raises D to D-sharp, creating a leading tone and an augmented second between C and D-sharp. Conventional ascending melodic minor raises C as well, producing C-sharp and D-sharp; descent commonly returns to natural minor in the textbook pattern. These forms describe resources used within minor tonality. Texture is a separate dimension: octave doubling can thicken a sound without creating independent melodic lines.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare E harmonic minor with ascending E melodic minor.
steps: Harmonic minor is E F-sharp G A B C D-sharp E.
Ascending melodic minor raises the sixth too: E F-sharp G A B C-sharp D-sharp E.
workedExamples.conclusion: The sixth differs; both forms contain the raised leading tone.

flashcards.front: Which degree is raised in harmonic minor?
Which additional degree rises in conventional ascending melodic minor?
What is E minor's leading tone?
Does octave doubling create polyphony?
flashcards.back: Not by itself; independence of lines matters.

diagrams.title: Two minor resources
diagrams.description: The raised sixth changes the approach to the leading tone.

modules.title: Spell chords before naming inversions
modules.focus: Separate a chord’s root from its bass.
explanation: A triad stacks two thirds. A major triad combines a major third and minor third above the root; a minor triad reverses that order. A dominant seventh chord adds a minor seventh above the root of a major triad.

Inversion depends on the lowest sounding chord member, not the top note. Root position places the root in the bass; first inversion places the third there; second inversion places the fifth there. Rearranging upper voices without changing the bass does not create a new inversion.

workedExample.prompt: Name E-G-C with E as the lowest note in C major.
steps: Reorder the pitch classes as C-E-G to identify a C major triad.
E is the third in the bass, so the chord is I6, first inversion.

misconception.claim: The lowest note is always the root.
misconception.correction: In an inversion the root remains the same while another chord member is lowest.

questions.prompt: Spell a G dominant seventh chord.
questions.hint: Build a major triad and add a minor seventh.
questions.answer: G B D F.

questions.prompt: Name the inversion of C-E-A with C lowest.
questions.answer: A minor in first inversion: A-C-E with its third C in the bass.
checkpoints: Uses the bass to name inversion

questions.prompt: Name A-C-F with A lowest in F major.
questions.answer: The triad is F-A-C, F major. A is its third. It is I6, first inversion.
checkpoints: The triad is F-A-C, F major.

questions.prompt: Name F-G-B-D with F lowest in C major.
hints: Locate the seventh in the bass.
questions.answer: The chord is G7. F is its seventh. It is V4/2, third inversion.

notes.title: Spell chords before naming inversions in depth
paragraphs: Chord quality is determined from the root before inversion is assigned. A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds, while an augmented triad stacks two major thirds. The bass then identifies which chord member is lowest. Seventh chords have four possible inversions: root position, first inversion with the third in the bass, second with the fifth and third with the seventh. Figured-bass abbreviations 7, 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2 correspond to those positions. An enharmonic respelling can change the apparent interval structure, so retain the spelling required by the harmonic context.

workedExamples.prompt: Identify B-D-F-G with B in the bass, in C major.
steps: Reorder as G-B-D-F: a G dominant seventh chord.
B is its third, so this is first inversion, V6/5.
workedExamples.conclusion: The root remains G even though B is the lowest note.

flashcards.front: What makes a diminished triad?
What makes an augmented triad?
What is the bass of a third-inversion seventh chord?
What figure denotes first-inversion seventh?

diagrams.title: Root and bass
diagrams.description: Reordering identifies the chord; the sounding bass identifies inversion.

nodes.label: V6/5
nodes.detail: Third B in the bass gives first inversion.

modules.title: Hear function through written resolution
modules.focus: Use leading tones and chord sevenths purposefully.
explanation: In common-practice tonal harmony, tonic establishes a point of rest and dominant creates an expectation of return. At a V7-I resolution, the leading tone typically moves upward to tonic and the chordal seventh downward by step. Voice-leading rules describe this style, not every musical tradition.

Analyse each voice horizontally as well as each chord vertically. Correct chord spelling does not prevent awkward leaps, crossed voices or parallel perfect intervals. A cadence is a phrase-ending harmonic event; a perfect authentic cadence also depends on root-position V-I and tonic in the final soprano.

workedExample.prompt: Resolve the tendency tones B and F from G7 to C major.
steps: In C major B is the leading tone, so move it up to C.
F is the dominant chord’s seventh, so move it down to E.

misconception.claim: Any V-I progression is a perfect authentic cadence.
misconception.correction: Its phrase placement, inversions and final soprano also matter.

questions.prompt: Where does F normally resolve in G7-C?
questions.answer: Down by step to E in the common-practice resolution.

questions.prompt: A phrase ends on V in C major. Name the cadence.
questions.answer: A half cadence.

questions.prompt: Resolve F-sharp and C from D7 to G major.
questions.answer: F-sharp normally rises to G. C normally falls to B. The motions resolve V7's tendency tones into G-major harmony.
checkpoints: The motions resolve V7's tendency tones into G-major harmony.

questions.prompt: A phrase ends with root-position V–I but scale degree three in the soprano. Is it a perfect authentic cadence?
questions.answer: It is not a perfect authentic cadence. The soprano does not end on tonic. In the described tonal context it is an imperfect authentic cadence.
checkpoints: It is not a perfect authentic cadence.
The soprano does not end on tonic.
In the described tonal context it is an imperfect authentic cadence.

notes.title: Hear function through written resolution in depth
paragraphs: Voice leading connects individual parts across harmonies. In a standard V7–I resolution, the leading tone tends upward to tonic and the chordal seventh downward by step, but chord completeness and voicing can affect the full realisation. Check outer-voice motion and each pair of parts for unintended parallel perfect intervals in the style being studied. A cadence label also depends on phrase position. A V–I progression in the middle of a phrase is not automatically a cadence, and an authentic cadence is perfect only when its required root positions and final soprano tonic are present.

workedExamples.prompt: Resolve the tendency tones C-sharp and G from A7 to D major.
steps: A7 is A-C-sharp-E-G; C-sharp is D major's leading tone.
Move C-sharp to D and the chordal seventh G down to F-sharp.
workedExamples.conclusion: Those resolutions support V7–I; the remaining voices still require checking.

flashcards.front: What is D major's leading tone?
Where does G usually resolve from A7 to D?
Does every V–I form a cadence?
What final soprano note is required for a perfect authentic cadence?

diagrams.title: Tendency-tone resolution
diagrams.description: The two directed motions support a tonic arrival.

nodes.label: D major
nodes.detail: D and F-sharp are reached within tonic harmony.

modules.title: Prepare the dominant
explanation: Predominant harmony commonly leads toward dominant. In a major key, ii and IV often fill this role. Roman numerals show scale-degree roots and chord quality, while figured-bass symbols identify inversions. Harmonic function depends on context as well as a chord label.

A cadential six-four commonly places tonic-triad pitches above the dominant bass before V. In that context its upper notes behave as embellishments of dominant harmony: the fourth above the bass resolves to a third and the sixth to a fifth. Labelling its pitches I6/4 alone does not explain its function.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse D-F-A, G-B-D, C-E-G in C major.
steps: Identify roots D, G and C as degrees 2, 5 and 1.
Label ii-V-I and explain the progression as predominant, dominant and tonic.

misconception.claim: Every tonic triad has tonic function.
misconception.correction: A cadential six-four can serve dominant expansion because of its bass and resolutions.

questions.prompt: Spell IV in G major.
questions.answer: C E G.

questions.prompt: In C major, C and E sound over bass G before B and D over G. Describe the upper motion.
questions.answer: The fourth C moves to the third B; the sixth E moves to the fifth D.

questions.prompt: Label A-C-E, D-F-sharp-A, G-B-D in G major.
questions.answer: The progression is ii–V–I. A minor functions as predominant and D major as dominant. G major supplies tonic resolution.
checkpoints: A minor functions as predominant and D major as dominant.

questions.prompt: Why is a cadential six-four not adequately explained as a stable tonic chord?
questions.answer: Its bass is usually dominant. The fourth and sixth resolve as embellishments. Its phrase function therefore prepares or prolongs dominant rather than providing stable tonic rest.
checkpoints: The fourth and sixth resolve as embellishments.
Its phrase function therefore prepares or prolongs dominant rather than providing stable tonic rest.

notes.title: Prepare the dominant in depth
paragraphs: Predominant harmonies prepare dominant through both root relationships and voice leading. In a major key, ii6 often places scale degree four in the bass and moves smoothly towards V. A cadential six-four uses tonic-triad pitches above a dominant bass, but its function is usually understood as an embellishment of dominant. Above that bass, the sixth commonly moves to the fifth and the fourth to the third. Distinguish the chord's pitch collection from its role in the phrase. A label that names only tonic pitches misses the directed resolutions that create the cadence.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse a cadential six-four in G major: bass D, upper notes G and B, resolving to F-sharp and A over D.
steps: G is a fourth above D and B a sixth.
G moves to F-sharp, 4–3; B moves to A, 6–5.
workedExamples.conclusion: The upper voices embellish dominant harmony before a possible tonic arrival.

flashcards.front: What is ii in G major?
What bass supports G major's cadential six-four?
What is its typical 4–3 motion?
Why does pitch spelling alone not determine function?

diagrams.title: Cadential six-four in G
diagrams.description: A dominant bass supports directed upper-voice resolutions.

nodes.label: D bass with G and B
G tonic arrival
nodes.detail: A possible completion of the cadence.

modules.title: Identify embellishing tones
modules.focus: Use approach, departure and metric placement.
explanation: A non-chord tone is understood against the harmony sounding beneath it. A passing tone connects two chord tones by step in the same direction. A neighbour tone leaves a chord tone by step and returns to it. A suspension is prepared, held into a new harmony, then resolves, usually downward by step.

Do not label every unfamiliar note as a wrong note or identify embellishments from pitch alone. Establish the chord and track the melodic motion. Motives can also return at a new pitch level or with changed rhythm; describe what remains recognisable and what changes.

workedExample.prompt: Over a sustained C major chord, a melody plays C-D-E.
steps: C and E belong to the chord while D does not.
The melody moves by step in one direction, so D is a passing tone.

misconception.claim: Any repeated non-chord note is a suspension.
misconception.correction: A suspension requires preparation and a held note across a harmonic change before resolution.

questions.prompt: Over C major, identify D in C-D-C.
questions.hint: Look at the return to the original pitch.
questions.answer: An upper neighbour tone.

questions.prompt: A short melody returns two scale steps higher with the same rhythm. What device is suggested?
questions.hint: Think of a repeated pattern at another level.
questions.answer: A melodic sequence, if the pattern is repeated at the new pitch level.

questions.prompt: Over sustained F major, label A-B-flat-C.
questions.answer: A and C are chord tones. B-flat connects them by step in one direction. B-flat is a passing tone.
checkpoints: A and C are chord tones.
B-flat connects them by step in one direction.

questions.prompt: Why cannot a held F over a C-major chord be called a suspension without earlier context?
questions.answer: F is dissonant against the stated chord in this context. Its preparation in the preceding harmony is unknown. Its resolution must also be inspected before assigning suspension.
checkpoints: F is dissonant against the stated chord in this context.
Its preparation in the preceding harmony is unknown.
Its resolution must also be inspected before assigning suspension.

notes.title: Identify embellishing tones in depth
paragraphs: An embellishing tone is defined by its relation to both harmony and melodic motion. A neighbour returns to its starting chord tone, while a passing tone continues between different chord tones. A suspension requires preparation, suspension into a changed harmony and resolution; a dissonance alone is not enough. Rhythmic placement helps distinguish accented from unaccented embellishments. Establish when the underlying chord changes before assigning a label. The same pitch can be a chord member in one harmony and a non-chord tone in another, so analysis must follow the musical timeline.

workedExamples.prompt: Over a held G-major triad, analyse B-C-B.
steps: B belongs to G-B-D, while C does not.
The melody steps away from B to C and returns to B.
workedExamples.conclusion: C is an upper neighbour, not a passing tone.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes a neighbour from a passing tone?
What three stages define a suspension?
Is C always a non-chord tone?
What is an accented embellishment?
flashcards.back: One occurring in a metrically accented position.

diagrams.title: Upper-neighbour motion
diagrams.description: The harmony stays G major throughout.

modules.title: Explain a secondary dominant
explanation: A secondary dominant is the dominant of a diatonic chord other than tonic. In C major, D major can function as V/V because D-F-sharp-A leads to G. The F-sharp acts as a local leading tone to G even though it is outside the C major key signature.

Tonicisation briefly gives a chord tonic-like emphasis. Modulation establishes a new key more durably through phrase structure and cadential evidence. One chromatic chord alone is insufficient to claim a modulation. Spell the target chord first, then build its dominant and check the actual resolution.

steps: D7 contains D-F-sharp-A-C and points toward G.
Label V7/V-V-I: G is temporarily tonicised before the phrase returns to C.

misconception.claim: Every accidental proves a change of key.
misconception.correction: Accidentals can embellish a line or create brief tonicisation without establishing a new key.

questions.prompt: Spell V/ii in C major.
questions.hint: The target ii is D minor; find D’s dominant.
questions.answer: A C-sharp E, an A major triad.

questions.prompt: Where does F-sharp tend to move in D7-G?
questions.hint: Treat G as the local tonic.
questions.answer: Up by semitone to G.

questions.prompt: Identify C7–F in C major.
questions.hint: Treat F as a local target.
hints: Treat F as a local target.
questions.answer: C7 is C-E-G-B-flat. It functions as V7/IV when resolving to F. F remains IV in the prevailing key unless further evidence establishes modulation.
checkpoints: It functions as V7/IV when resolving to F.
F remains IV in the prevailing key unless further evidence establishes modulation.

questions.prompt: Why does F-sharp in C major not automatically mean the music has changed to G major?
questions.hint: An accidental has several possible roles.
hints: An accidental has several possible roles.
questions.answer: It could be a local leading tone in tonicisation or another chromatic event. A sustained new tonal centre needs broader harmonic evidence. Cadences and continued function help distinguish modulation.
checkpoints: It could be a local leading tone in tonicisation or another chromatic event.
A sustained new tonal centre needs broader harmonic evidence.
Cadences and continued function help distinguish modulation.

notes.title: Explain a secondary dominant in depth
paragraphs: A secondary dominant is built from the temporary target's key, then interpreted within the prevailing key. In G major, an A7 chord contains C-sharp and points towards D, so it can function as V7/V. The altered note is meaningful because of its directed resolution, not merely because it is absent from the key signature. A secondary leading-tone chord can likewise tonicise a diatonic target. Distinguish brief tonicisation from a durable key change using phrase structure, cadences and continued harmonic behaviour; a single accidental does not establish modulation.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse E7–A minor–D7–G in G major.
steps: E7 contains E-G-sharp-B-D and points to A minor, the ii chord.
Label E7 as V7/ii, followed by ii–V7–I.
workedExamples.conclusion: A minor receives brief emphasis before the progression returns towards G.

flashcards.front: What is V7/V in G major?
What does E7 tonicise in G major?
What does G-sharp tend towards in E7–A minor?
Does one chromatic chord prove modulation?

diagrams.title: Tonicising ii in G
diagrams.description: The progression temporarily directs attention to A minor.

nodes.label: D7–G
nodes.detail: Dominant-to-tonic motion in the prevailing key.

modules.title: Compare modes and phrase designs
modules.focus: Distinguish pitch collection from formal return.
explanation: A mode has a tonic and a characteristic interval pattern. D Dorian uses D-E-F-G-A-B-C-D; its raised sixth relative to D natural minor is B-natural. Playing white notes without establishing a tonal centre does not by itself communicate a particular mode.

Form describes relationships across spans of music. In binary form two principal sections are often labelled A and B. Ternary form returns to A after a contrasting B. Repetition signs, cadences, thematic material and key areas all contribute to analysis; section length alone is not decisive.

workedExample.prompt: Compare D Dorian with D natural minor, then describe A-B-A.
steps: Only the sixth differs: Dorian has B-natural and natural minor has B-flat.
A-B-A suggests ternary organisation when the final A restores recognisable opening material.

misconception.claim: Any three phrases create ternary form.
misconception.correction: Ternary form depends on contrasting and returning material, not simply counting phrases.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes C Mixolydian from C major?
questions.answer: C Mixolydian has B-flat rather than B-natural.

questions.prompt: Why might A-A-B-B still be binary?
questions.answer: It contains two principal sections, each repeated, rather than four distinct formal sections.

questions.prompt: Spell A Dorian and compare it with A natural minor.
questions.hint: Use Dorian's raised sixth relative to natural minor.
hints: Use Dorian's raised sixth relative to natural minor.
questions.answer: A Dorian is A B C D E F-sharp G A. A natural minor has F-natural. The sixth is the differing degree.
checkpoints: A Dorian is A B C D E F-sharp G A.
The sixth is the differing degree.

questions.prompt: Why is a four-bar return of an opening motive not enough by itself to classify a whole work as ternary?
questions.hint: A motive is smaller than a section.
hints: A motive is smaller than a section.
questions.answer: The return may occur within another formal design. Section boundaries and contrasting spans need analysis. Cadential and thematic context determines the larger organisation.
checkpoints: The return may occur within another formal design.
Section boundaries and contrasting spans need analysis.
Cadential and thematic context determines the larger organisation.

notes.title: Compare modes and phrase designs in depth
paragraphs: Mode analysis requires a tonal centre as well as a pitch collection. G Mixolydian uses G A B C D E F G, differing from G major at the seventh degree. The pitch F alone does not establish that mode if the music still centres elsewhere. Formal analysis similarly depends on relationships, not labels attached to equal lengths. A return can be recognisable even when shortened or varied. Compare thematic material, cadential closure and tonal plan to decide whether a final section restores an opening idea or merely repeats a small motive within another design.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare G Mixolydian and G major, then analyse a hypothetical A–B–A′ design.
steps: G Mixolydian has F-natural; G major has F-sharp. Both require G as centre for that comparison.
A′ restores recognisable A material with changes, so the plan suggests varied ternary organisation.
workedExamples.conclusion: Pitch collection and formal return need contextual confirmation.

flashcards.front: What differs between G Mixolydian and G major?
What does A′ indicate?
flashcards.back: A recognisable but varied return of A.

flashcards.front: Does a shared pitch collection prove a shared centre?
What helps establish formal sections?
flashcards.back: Themes, cadences, tonal areas and returns.

diagrams.title: Varied ternary return
diagrams.description: A final section can restore identity without exact repetition.

nodes.label: A′
nodes.detail: Opening material returns in altered form.
